items.content_excerpt: $AMD $SPY $QQQ $AMDL Baird analyst Tristan Gerra's $1250 price target on AMD was the first truly aggressive upgrade on the Street. While the target appears extreme relative to current consensus estimates, it is not as implausible as many investors assume, particularly given the rapidly evolving AI compute landscape. Gerra's thesis is built on the assumption that AMD can leverage its growing leadership in both AI CPUs and GPUs to capture approximately 15% of a projected $1.4 trillion AI compute total addressable market (TAM) by 2030. Under that framework, AMD's earnings power could expand dramatically, with EPS exceeding $50 per share by the end of the decade. Notably, Gerra is not alone in projecting this level of earnings growth. Piper Sandler has similarly modeled AMD's EPS compounding at roughly 65% annually, reaching the low-$50 range by 2030.

items.title: $APLD Yes, I’ve read what’s public as part of my DD. Only the $CRWV leases have been publicly disclosed and filed with the SEC although of c
items.content_excerpt: $APLD Yes, I’ve read what’s public as part of my DD. Only the $CRWV leases have been publicly disclosed and filed with the SEC although of course they are in redacted form. The contents of the other leases have been disclosed in $APLD filings in terms of the characterizations of them. And yes, tenants CAN terminate the leases IF $APLD misses the delivery deadlines in the contracts. $CRWV and $ORCL both have that protection. There are grace periods, possible extensions and notice requirements, so missing a target date doesn’t automatically give the tenant a way out. For $CRWV’s first two leases, $APLD specifically says a qualifying delivery failure can let the tenant terminate the lease without a termination fee or further lease payments. For the remaining 150 MW building, there is a July 29, 2027 deadline for the first three halls to meet the required commencement conditions. Some of the details are redacted, so I wouldn’t pretend we can see every exception. For $ORCL, there is a cancellation right if delivery runs more than 150 days late against phased dates starting October 1, 2026. Fitch also reports an $ORCL parent guarantee and rights to terminate for chronic outages. But $ORCL’s actual agreements are not public, so I don’t know every notice requirement or exactly what $ORCL would owe when using one of those exits. For the $META projects at Delta Forge 1, Delta Forge 2 and Polaris Forge 3, I’ve read the public disclosures. I haven’t seen the actual tenant leases which are NOT available. To be clear, $APLD has never acknowledged $META as the tenant but Wells Fargo reported it, and I have reported it too from mine and other’s examinations of the publicly available filings. ￼ We know $APLD acknowledges construction-delay cancellation risk, but we don’t have those projects’ specific deadlines, exceptions or guarantee terms. I’m not going to claim I’ve reviewed clauses that haven’t been released. If a tenant simply changes its plans, that’s expensive. APLD says voluntary cancellation by the tenant requires payment of the entire remaining contract value. $CRWV’s clause is explicit: 100% of the remaining scheduled base rent, plus specified taxes, paid before the cancellation takes effect. That payment requirement is separate from its rights to terminate the lease for delivery failures, uncured $APLD defaults, major property damage or condemnation. The lease values are roughly $11B for $CRWV , $5B for $ORCL and $20.2B across the $META projects, over 15 years. Most have three optional five-year renewals; $ORCL has two. I count the roughly $36B of initial-term commitments separately from the much larger $85 billion figure that assumes every renewal gets exercised. There are also protections in the later $CRWV arrangements. Some leases moved to a subsidiary, with parent guarantees that kick in under specified circumstances. At ELN-02, if the subsidiary’s lease ends, the suspended parent lease resumes for those halls. Moving the lease into a subsidiary doesn’t, by itself, make the parent’s commitment disappear. As we all know, the KEY factor to $APLD raking in this huge pile of revenue is on time construction execution. So far, $APLD has executed its construction milestones flawlessly. There’s no guarantee $APLD will continue to do that but I’m quite optimistic given it’s spotless to date track record. $APLD already has the first 250 MW for $CRWV operating at Polaris Forge 1 and has projected completing another 600 MW within the next 12 months. These lease contracts make it expensive for tenants to change their minds, but $APLD still must finish the remaining buildings on time and keep them running as promised. I take the backlog seriously. The delivery deadlines are part of the deal too.

items.content_excerpt: @meszaros I agree, excellent, detailed analysis. However, the Section 834 discussion regarding the third-country-melt loophole deserves an update, since this was published June 6, 2026. On July 20, President Trump signed an executive order directing the Pentagon to trace critical defense supply chains back to raw-material origins, including subcontractors at every tier. I believe this could substantially reduce, if not ultimately eliminate, the ability to circumvent sourcing restrictions by processing Chinese-origin materials in third countries. While not explicitly closing the Section 834 loophole as Section 854's rules did, this is arguably the strongest evidence yet that the government intends to close it completely. Combined with Sam Rubin's February comments and LightPath's January NDAA announcement, I believe this strengthens the regulatory outlook for $LPTH and addresses one of the analysis's biggest uncertainties.

items.content_excerpt: $RBLX RBLX is higher today mainly on better-than-expected third-quarter engagement, led by the viral game Steal an Egg, plus a Wedbush estimate hike ahead of earnings. Wedbush said Q3 activity came in stronger than it modeled. The firm raised its Q3 bookings estimate to $1.7 billion from $1.64 billion and EBITDA to $215 million from $193 million. Third-party data it cited showed total platform hours down only 7% year over year, versus the 16% drop Wedbush had expected. Excluding a fading group of older hits, hours were up 37% year over year, accelerating from 20% in Q2. Steal an Egg hit peak daily hours comparable to last year’s big titles (Grow a Garden and Steal a Brainrot), though engagement on it has already started to roll over. That matters because tighter safety controls earlier in 2026 — the global rollout of Roblox Kids and Roblox Select accounts — had weighed on users and bookings.
